units.t: Music. Episode two.
In this episode: The Stradivarius mystery, A guide to classical music, Opera, explained: drama at full volume and The night The Rite of Spring caused an uproar.
Part one. The Stradivarius mystery.
Violins made in a small Italian town three centuries ago sell for millions of dollars.
But when top players are blindfolded, can they actually tell the difference?
The master of Cremona.
Cremona, in northern Italy, was the heart of violin making for generations.
The Amati family established the craft there in the 1500s, and the Guarneri family also worked in town.
Antonio Stradivari was born around 1644 and may have trained with Nicolò Amati.
He worked for an extraordinary length of time, making violins, violas, cellos, guitars and harps until he died in 1737, in his early nineties.
Estimates suggest he made a thousand or more instruments, and roughly 650 are thought to survive, though the numbers are approximate.
Experts generally regard instruments from about 1700 to 1720 as his golden period, when his designs were most refined.
Searching for the secret.
A string alone makes little sound.
Its vibrations pass through the bridge into the body, a thin spruce top and maple back, which amplifies and shapes the tone.
Tiny differences in wood density, thickness and varnish change which frequencies are boosted.
People have long hunted for a lost secret.
One theory points to the Maunder Minimum, a period of low solar activity in the Little Ice Age, when slow-growing trees may have produced unusually dense wood.
Other research suggests the wood was treated with minerals or chemicals, perhaps against woodworm.
None is proven, and many experts think Stradivari's skill matters more than any single ingredient.
The blindfold tests.
From 2010, the French acoustics researcher Claudia Fritz and American violin maker Joseph Curtin ran careful experiments.
In the first, published in 2012, experienced violinists wore modified welder's goggles so they could not see which instrument they were playing.
They tried violins by Stradivari and Guarneri alongside high quality new ones.
Players could not reliably tell old from new, and the most preferred instrument was a new one.
A larger 2014 follow-up with leading soloists found similar results, and later concert hall tests found listeners often thought the new violins projected better.
These studies do not prove old violins are poor, only that their superiority is far less obvious than legend suggests.
Why the legend endures.
If blindfolded players struggle to pick them, why do Stradivari violins stay so valuable?
They are rare historical objects, like Old Master paintings, and their price reflects scarcity, craftsmanship and provenance as much as sound.
Many have names and long histories, passing through the hands of famous musicians.
Some violinists argue that lab tests cannot capture what it feels like to live with an instrument for years, learning its responses in large halls.
Belief may play a part too.
Knowing you are playing a three hundred year old masterpiece can change how you play and how listeners hear.
Researchers still debate how much of the magic is acoustic and how much is psychological.
Million-dollar instruments.
In 2011, the Stradivari known as the Lady Blunt sold for about 15.
9 million US dollars, with the proceeds going to relief efforts after the earthquake and tsunami in Japan.
Few working musicians could ever afford such prices, so many of the finest instruments are owned by banks, foundations, governments or wealthy collectors, who lend them to talented performers.
In Australia, for example, some leading players perform on historic Italian instruments on loan.
A few are kept almost unplayed in museums, such as the Messiah violin at the Ashmolean Museum in Oxford, prized partly because it looks nearly new.
Most are still played, which many musicians feel is what they were made for.
The key idea: Antonio Stradivari worked in Cremona into his early nineties, and his instruments from about 1700 to 1720 are called his golden period.
Part two. A guide to classical music.
Three centuries, three giants and a lot of music that still turns up in films, ads and ringtones.
Here is how to find your way in.
What 'classical' means.
In everyday speech, 'classical music' means the tradition of Western art music written for orchestras, choirs, soloists and small ensembles over roughly the last four centuries.

Historians divide it into periods: the Baroque, about 1600 to 1750; the Classical period, about 1750 to 1820, which confusingly gives the whole tradition its name; and the Romantic period, about 1820 to 1900.
Then came a burst of twentieth-century experiment.
The dates are rough, since composers did not wake up in a new era.
Knowing the periods helps you hear why a piece sounds the way it does.
Baroque and Bach.
Baroque music is busy, decorated and driven by a continuous bass line, often a cello with a harpsichord filling in chords.
Opera was born in Italy around 1600, and the concerto flourished.
Vivaldi's The Four Seasons, 1725, paints spring birdsong and winter ice in four violin concertos.
Handel's Messiah, first performed in Dublin in 1742, is still sung by Australian choirs every Christmas.
Johann Sebastian Bach, 1685 to 1750, was better known as an organist than a composer.
He wrote more than a thousand works, including the Brandenburg Concertos and the Mass in B minor.
His gift was counterpoint: several independent melodies played at once that fit together, as in a fugue.
His music fell from fashion until Mendelssohn revived the St Matthew Passion in 1829.
Classical clarity and Mozart.
After the dense layers of the Baroque, composers turned to clarity: a clear melody over simpler accompaniment, in balanced phrases.
The piano replaced the harpsichord.
This was the age of the symphony and the string quartet.
Haydn wrote more than 100 symphonies and is often called the father of both.
Sonata form, which presents two contrasting themes, develops them and brings them back, shaped instrumental music for 150 years.
Mozart, 1756 to 1791, toured Europe as a child prodigy from age six.
In 35 years he wrote over 600 works, including 41 symphonies and operas like The Marriage of Figaro and The Magic Flute.
He died in Vienna working on his Requiem.
The film Amadeus popularised a murderous rivalry with Salieri that historians don't support.
Beethoven and the Romantics.
Beethoven, 1770 to 1827, began losing his hearing in his late twenties and was almost completely deaf by his final years.
In 1802 he wrote a despairing letter, the Heiligenstadt Testament, yet kept composing.
His Fifth Symphony opens with perhaps the most famous four notes in music, and his Ninth, 1824, added singers to its finale.
His music was more personal and dramatic than that of earlier composers.
Romantic composers valued feeling and imagination over balance.
Orchestras and pieces grew larger, often linked to stories or landscapes.
Chopin wrote intimate piano music, Tchaikovsky the ballets Swan Lake and The Nutcracker, Wagner operas of four or five hours.
Dvořák and Grieg drew on folk music.
Today's sweeping film scores grow out of this era.
How to start listening.
You don't need training to enjoy classical music.
Start with short, well-known pieces: a movement of Vivaldi's The Four Seasons, Mozart's Eine kleine Nachtmusik, the opening of Beethoven's Fifth, or Tchaikovsky's Nutcracker suite.
Many are free on streaming services and on radio such as ABC Classic.
Listen actively the first time, with no phone, and notice what repeats and what changes.
If a piece grabs you, explore more by the same composer.
Then try it live: the Sydney, Melbourne and other state symphony orchestras run affordable concerts, and hearing a full orchestra in person is a different experience from headphones.
The key idea: 'Classical music' usually means the Western art music tradition, grouped into broad periods that explain how a piece sounds.
Part three. Opera, explained: drama at full volume.
Opera combines music, theatre, poetry, costume and spectacle, and its singers fill huge halls without microphones.
Here is how the most extravagant art form began and how to enjoy it.
Reviving the Greeks.
In the late 1500s scholars, poets and musicians in Florence, the Florentine Camerata, became fascinated by Greek tragedy.
They believed, partly correctly, that Greek plays were sung or chanted, and tried setting drama to music with a single voice singing clearly over simple accompaniment.
This led to the first operas around 1600.
The earliest still regularly staged is Monteverdi's L'Orfeo, first performed in Mantua in 1607, retelling the myth of Orpheus in the underworld.
Early operas were for princes at court.
In 1637 the first public opera house opened in Venice, and anyone with a ticket could attend.
Audiences chatted, ate and played cards.
Baroque stars included castrati, male singers castrated before puberty, a cruel practice that died out in the nineteenth century.
The words you need.
A little vocabulary helps enormously.
The libretto, meaning 'little book', is the opera's text, written by a librettist, while the composer writes the music.
Many operas begin with an overture, an orchestral piece that sets the mood before the curtain rises.
Much of the story moves forward in recitative, singing close to the rhythms of speech, often lightly accompanied, where plot and conversation happen.
Then the action pauses for an aria, a solo song in which a character expresses feelings at length, where singers show off.
Duets, trios and larger ensembles let several characters sing at once, sometimes each with different words and emotions, something spoken theatre cannot easily do.
The chorus represents crowds, soldiers, villagers or spirits.
The great composers.
Mozart, writing in the 1780s and early 1790s, gave opera human characters: The Marriage of Figaro, Don Giovanni and The Magic Flute.
In the early nineteenth century Rossini, Bellini and Donizetti perfected bel canto, 'beautiful singing', with dazzling vocal agility.
Verdi, Rigoletto, La Traviata, Aida, and Puccini, La Boheme, Tosca, Madama Butterfly, combined thrilling melodies with intense drama, and remain among the most performed.
They make good starting points.
Richard Wagner wanted opera as a total work of art.
His four-opera Ring cycle takes around fifteen hours.
Short musical themes, leitmotifs, represent characters and ideas, a technique film composers borrowed.
His Bayreuth theatre, opened in 1876, hid the orchestra and darkened the hall, helping create modern quiet, dark audiences.
His antisemitic writings make him a troubling figure.
Filling a hall unamplified.
An opera singer may need to be heard over dozens of players in a theatre seating a couple of thousand people, without a microphone.
Part of the answer is training: years developing breath control and an efficient, open throat.
Another part is acoustics.

Researchers have found that trained classical singers, particularly men, often produce a concentration of energy at high frequencies, around three thousand cycles per second, sometimes called the singer's formant.
An orchestra is comparatively quiet in that range, and human ears are especially sensitive to it, so the voice carries over the instruments.
Voices are classified by range, high to low: soprano, mezzo-soprano and contralto for women, and tenor, baritone and bass for men.
Composers write roles for particular voice types.
Opera in Australia.
Australia has a proud opera tradition.
Helen Porter Mitchell, born in Melbourne in 1861, took the stage name Nellie Melba in honour of her home city and became one of the world's most celebrated sopranos.
Peach Melba and Melba toast were named after her.
Joan Sutherland, born in Sydney in 1926, became a superstar of bel canto opera, nicknamed La Stupenda.
The main opera theatre at the Sydney Opera House bears her name.
Today Opera Australia is the national company, and state companies perform around the country.
If opera seems intimidating, remember that most performances show translated text as surtitles above the stage, a practice that spread from the 1980s, so you can follow every word.
The key idea: Opera began in Italy around 1600 in an attempt to recreate sung Greek drama, and public opera houses made it popular.
Part four. The night The Rite of Spring caused an uproar.
In Paris in 1913, a new ballet about an ancient sacrifice provoked jeers, shouting and scuffles in the audience.
Within a year, its music was being cheered.
Ballets Russes, pagan rites.
Before the First World War, Europe's most exciting dance company was the Ballets Russes, run by the Russian impresario Sergei Diaghilev.
His star dancer was Vaslav Nijinsky, and his young composer was Igor Stravinsky, who had already scored hits in Paris with The Firebird, 1910, and Petrushka, 1911.
With the painter Nicholas Roerich, Stravinsky devised a ballet about pagan rituals in prehistoric Russia, with Nijinsky as choreographer.
The Rite of Spring has no conventional plot.
Tribes celebrate spring with dances, and a young woman is chosen for sacrifice.
In the Sacrificial Dance she dances in a frenzy until she dies.
It premiered on 29 May 1913 at the new Théâtre des Champs-Élysées in Paris.
Music like nothing before.
The music opens with a bassoon playing a folk-like melody so high in its range that many listeners could not identify the instrument.
Soon the orchestra builds layers of overlapping tunes.
Then comes a famous passage where strings hammer the same harsh chord again and again, with accents falling in unpredictable places, so the listener cannot settle into a regular beat.
Elsewhere the time signature changes almost every bar.
Stravinsky used a very large orchestra, with extra woodwinds, brass and percussion.
Many melodies were based on or inspired by Russian folk tunes, but they were reshaped into something entirely new and startling.
Dancing against ballet.
Classical ballet prized elegance: turned-out feet, lifted bodies and the illusion of weightlessness.
Nijinsky did the opposite.
His dancers turned their toes inwards, hunched their shoulders, jumped heavily, landed with a thud and stamped in rhythmic groups.
Roerich's costumes were heavy, colourful smocks inspired by old Russian peasant dress.
To many in the audience it looked ugly or even ridiculous, and to others daringly modern.
The dancers found the shifting rhythms extremely hard to follow.
Nijinsky's choreography was performed only a handful of times and then largely lost, until it was reconstructed for the Joffrey Ballet in 1987 from notes, drawings and memories.
Uproar in the theatre.
Soon after the curtain rose, parts of the audience began to laugh, whistle and jeer, while others shouted back in defence of the work.
The noise grew so loud that the dancers struggled to hear the orchestra, and Nijinsky stood on a chair in the wings shouting the counts to them.
Stravinsky left his seat and went backstage.
Exactly what happened is hard to pin down.
Many famous descriptions were written years or decades later and contradict each other.
Some describe fist fights and objects being thrown, and stories circulated of police being called.
Historians agree there was a real uproar, but caution that the legend of a full-scale riot has probably grown.
From scandal to classic.
The ballet was performed only a few more times in 1913.
But in April 1914 the music was played as a concert piece in Paris without dancers, and this time it was a triumph, with Stravinsky reportedly carried from the hall on admirers' shoulders.
Freed from the startling choreography, audiences could focus on the score's raw power.
The Rite became one of the most influential works of the century, shaping later classical music, jazz and film scores.
In 1940, Walt Disney used it in the film Fantasia, set to scenes of the early Earth and dinosaurs.
Today it is a regular part of orchestral programmes, and dozens of choreographers have created their own versions of the ballet.
The key idea: The Rite of Spring was a Ballets Russes work about ancient pagan rituals, ending with a young woman dancing herself to death.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. What do experts mean by Stradivari's 'golden period'?
Answer. The years when his designs were most refined.
Question two. What does knowing the main periods of classical music help you do?
Answer. Hear why a piece sounds the way it does.
Question three. Why did the Florentine Camerata create the first operas?
Answer. They wanted to recreate ancient Greek drama as sung.
Question four. What happens in the ballet's final scene?
Answer. A chosen young woman dances in a frenzy until she dies.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
